name: Dice Rolls
content:
There are four main kinds of dice rolls in Renaissance: Skill Checks, Engagement Rolls, Damage Rolls and Luck Checks. The most common are Skill Checks:

SKILL CHECKS

When a character decides to take action and the outcome is uncertain, they make a SKILL CHECK.

To make a Skill Check, roll one feat die (d12) and a number of additional success dice (d6) determined by a character’s prowess in a given Skill (see Core Stats). Add together all the dice to determine the result:

= 14

The result is then compared against an opposing roll, a static target, or is interpreted subjectively by the GM.

OPPOSED SKILL CHECKS

If a character's action is actively opposed by another character or creature, it is typically an OPPOSED SKILL CHECK. The opponent rolls a Skill Check of their own and the two results are compared to determine the winner. On a tie, both sides re-roll.

Many character Abilities call for Opposed Skill Checks, specifying which Skills should be rolled. If the GM calls for an Opposed Skill Check, they determine which Skills each side must roll.

If there is no active opponent to the character's action, the result of the Skill Check is typically compared against a Difficulty:

SKILL CHECKS AGAINST DIFFICULTY

If a character’s action isn’t contested but must overcome environmental challenges or demonstrate competence in a Skill, the GM sets a DIFFICULTY for the Skill Check before the roll is made. If the result meets or exceeds the Difficulty, the check passes: the character does what they set out to do. Otherwise, it is a failure. Use the scale below as a guide when setting Difficulty:

If an action seems like it should have a Difficulty below 6, that’s an indication that there isn’t enough uncertainty involved to require a roll. The character does what they set out to do and the narrative moves forward.

If an action doesn't have a clear pass/fail outcome, the GM can choose to omit Difficulty and instead evaluate the roll result subjectively:

SUBJECTIVE SKILL CHECKS

Gathering information, observing your surroundings, social interaction - in situations like these, often the Skill Check is not determining whether an action is effective, but how effective it is. In these cases, the GM may simply see what the roll result is and react accordingly.

Alternatively, if they want to set some clear stakes, the GM can set multiple Difficulties with different outcomes attached to each Difficulty.

FAVORED & ILL-FAVORED

Various effects may call for a Skill Check to be FAVORED or ILL-FAVORED:

  • If a Skill Check is Favored, roll the feat die twice and keep the higher result.

  • If a Skill Check is Ill-Favored, roll the feat die twice and keep the lower result.

Either way, you only roll the success dice (if any) once and add them to the feat die result to get the overall result:

FAVORED result would be 15 (10+5), ILL-FAVORED result would be 9 (4+5).

Favored and Ill-Favored cancel each other out. If a roll is already Favored and an effect would make it Ill-favored, it becomes a flat roll - just roll the feat die once. Similarly, if a roll is already Ill-Favored and an effect would make it Favored, it becomes a flat roll.

DICE BONUSES & PENALTIES

Various effects may add or remove success dice from the pool for a Skill Check. Throughout the game rules, you'll see this expressed in a shorthand: "+1d" means "add one success die" to the Skill Check. "-2d" means "remove two success dice" from the Skill Check.

The maximum number of success dice for a Skill Check is 5. Taking +1d to a Skill Check that already includes 5 success dice has no effect.

The minimum is 0, but taking -1d to a Skill Check that already has 0 success dice does have an effect: it makes the Skill Check Ill-Favored. Additional -d penalties beyond that have no further effect.

DICE RESULTS

When determining the result of a Skill Check, there are special rules for both types of dice:

FEAT DIE (d12)

  • Rolling a 1-10 on a feat die simply adds that number to the Check’s total result.

  • Rolling a 12 on a feat die is Sol 🌞 - the best result:

    • The feat die adds 12 to the total roll result.

    • If you are in the Quest phase, the party moves one notch closer to Boon (see Per-Quest Mechanics).

  • Rolling an 11 on a feat die is Morte 💀 - the worst result:

    • The feat die adds 0 to the total roll result.

    • If you are in the Quest phase, the party moves one notch closer to Bane (see Per-Quest Mechanics) and the GM takes a Soft Move.

Note that it is possible to fail/lose a Skill Check with a result that includes Sol 🌞, and it is possible to pass/win a Skill Check with a result that includes Morte 💀. The outcome of the Check is still determined by comparing total results against a Difficulty or an opponent's Skill Check result.

When determining whether one feat die roll is higher than another, Morte 💀 is considered 0, not 11.

SUCCESS DICE (d6)

  • Rolling a 1-5 on a success die simply adds that number to the total roll result.

  • Rolling a 6✨ adds that number to the total roll result AND gives you a Success, which you can spend on various additional effects. Multiple 6✨s on a single roll means you have multiple Successes to spend:

SPENDING SUCCESSES

If a Skill Check contains one or more SUCCESSES, regardless of the outcome of the Check itself, you may spend each Success to achieve one additional effect. Many abilities have their own additional effects available that can be bought with Successes, but the following effects are always available to you:

  • Discover a secret.

  • Discover a weakness.

  • Discover a resource.

  • Take +1d on your next Skill Check.

  • Pass +1d to an Ally for their next Skill Check.

You cannot choose the same effect twice as part of the same Skill Check. The specifics of the three “discover” effects are determined and described by the GM. The specifics of the +1d effects are described by the player.

Unspent Successes are lost once the Skill Check is resolved.

Another way to spend Successes is to upgrade a failure to a Pass/Win With Consequence:

PASS/WIN WITH CONSEQUENCE

If the result of a Skill Check is a failure/loss but includes one or more Successes, the player may request (or the GM may offer) a PASS WITH CONSEQUENCE (against Difficulty) or WIN WITH CONSEQUENCE (Opposed Skill Check).

If the player and GM both accept, all of the Successes are considered spent, the Skill Check is upgraded to a pass/win, and the GM takes a Soft Move (see Phases of Play).

The severity of the Soft Move should be commensurate with how far below the Difficulty or opponent's result the check’s total result is. In extreme circumstances, the GM can even elect to upgrade to a Hard Move.

The GM is generally encouraged to accept reasonable requests for a Pass/Win With Consequence, but they have full discretion.

GROUP SKILL CHECK

When two or more characters attempt to overcome an obstacle as a group, the GM may call for a GROUP SKILL CHECK.

The GM sets a single Difficulty and all participants roll Skill Checks against that Difficulty to determine the outcome. The Skill Checks may all use the same skill or may vary, depending on the obstacle and how each character is contributing to the effort. The GM has discretion to accept or reject particular Skills as relevant.

A majority of passes means the Group Skill Check passes. A majority of failures means the Group Skill Check fails. If there is a tie, the player who rolled the lowest result has the dubious honor of rolling a Luck Check (see below) as a tiebreaker.

Any Successes rolled as part of a Group Skill Check are still individual to the character that rolled them - they are the only one who can spend the Successes.

However, on a group failure, if the total number of Successes rolled by all participants is equal to or greater than the number of characters involved, the group may request (or the GM may offer) a Pass With Consequence, as defined above.

ENGAGEMENT ROLLS

When two combatants engage in melee combat, there is a special step before each attack is resolved called ENGAGEMENT. In this step, each combatant rolls a variable number of dice to attempt to gain an advantage in the exchange. The interactions of the dice represent the maneuvers and footwork in hand-to-hand combat that precede an attempt to land a blow.

The rules of Engagement are fully explained in the Combat section.

DAMAGE ROLLS

Various Weapons, Abilities, and effects call for DAMAGE ROLLS to help determine their impact. Damage Rolls are made with varying sets of dice, determined by the Weapon, Ability, or effect that calls for the roll, and may include one or more dice of any type.

Similar to Skill Checks, Damage Rolls can be subject to bonuses and penalties, again represented by the same shorthand: +1d, +2d, -1d, -2d, etc. In the case, this means adding or removing damage dice from the dice pool.

Bonuses can increase the dice pool for a Damage roll to any size, and penalties can reduce the dice pool to 0 dice (but not negative dice).

Some abilities upgrade or downgrade damage dice by one or more steps. The chain is:

d4 ↔ d6 ↔ d8 ↔ d10 ↔ d12 ↔ d20

A damage die cannot be downgraded below d4 or upgraded above d20.

In general, you will add a modifier to the result of a damage roll. Typically the modifier will be one of your Core Stat scores (see the Core Stats section). If penalties reduce the dice pool for a Damage Roll to 0 dice, you still add together any modifiers to determine the result.

By default, the result of a Damage Roll determines the amount of Endurance the target loses (see the Core Stats section).

LUCK CHECKS

At their discretion, the GM may call for a LUCK CHECK to determine a variety of factors throughout gameplay that are not dependent on characters' actions.

To make a Luck Check, a player simply rolls one feat die. In general, a roll of 1-5 or Morte 💀 results in bad luck, while a roll of 6-10 or Sol 🌞 results in good luck. The GM may also choose to define other thresholds for specific outcomes.

Note that rolling Morte 💀 or Sol 🌞 on a Luck Check does move the Quest toward Bane/Boon as normal and - in the case of Morte 💀 - the GM takes a Soft Move as normal.

Luck Checks should never be used to replace character skills or abilities. They should be used to determine truly random environmental factors.
